title: Constant-colour polynomial-time colouring of 3-colourable graphs
formal: Do there exist an absolute integer \(C\geq3\) and a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm that, on every finite simple undirected graph promised to be \(3\)-colourable, outputs a proper colouring using at most \(C\) colours with probability at least \(2/3\)? The same palette bound and finite program must work for all graph sizes. This card retains the explicitly adopted randomized version of the constant-palette problem.
definitions:
The input is an explicit finite simple undirected graph \(G=([n],E)\), with \(n\geq1\), a unary size header and an adjacency matrix. There are no loops or parallel edges; isolated vertices count toward \(n\). The binary input length \(L\) is of order \(n^2+1\). The promise asserts the existence of a proper colouring with at most three colours, but supplies no colouring or other witness.

A proper \(k\)-colouring is a function \(c:[n]\to[k]\) with \(c(u)\ne c(v)\) for every edge \(\{u,v\}\). A successful output explicitly lists one binary colour index in \([C]\) for each vertex, in vertex order. The algorithm may instead output a failure symbol. A candidate can be checked against the palette bound and all edges in polynomial time; invalid candidates can be converted to failure. Successful runs must colour every vertex and leave no monochromatic edge.

Use one randomized multitape Turing machine \(A\) and fixed positive integers \(K,d\) such that every computation takes at most \(K(L+1)^d\) bit operations on every graph and every random-bit sequence. All arithmetic precision, output and random-bit generation are included. The random bits are independent and fair, there are polynomially many of them in each run, and the machine has no advice or oracle. Deterministic algorithms are included. No correctness or success-probability requirement is imposed outside the three-colourability promise, but the time bound still applies.

For every promised graph, the probability of a valid \(C\)-colouring must be at least \(2/3\), over the internal bits alone. This is a guarantee for each individual input, not an average over random graphs. The existentially chosen \(C,K,d,A\) are fixed before the graph: \(C\) cannot depend on \(n\), degree, density or the particular input. The exponent and constants may depend on the selected palette bound because only one constant palette is required. Independent repetition can amplify the success probability after checking outputs; exact recognition of the three-colourability promise is not required.

There is no planarity, bounded-degree, expansion, forbidden-subgraph, random-input or supplied-decomposition assumption. A palette of six, one hundred or any other fixed integer could establish a positive answer. A number of colours growing with \(n\), however slowly, does not satisfy the constant-palette requirement.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of existence of at least one such constant \(C\) and algorithm, or a proof in Lean that no such pair exists. A positive answer must verify all-input worst-case polynomial bit complexity and, for every promised graph, success probability at least \(2/3\) with a proper colouring of the full graph using that one palette.

A negative answer must exclude every absolute \(C\geq3\) and every uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm with the stated guarantee. Unconditional NP-hardness of each three-versus-\(C\) decision promise would give a complexity-theoretic obstruction, but deducing nonexistence of these randomized algorithms from it additionally requires \(\mathsf{NP}\ne\mathsf{RP}\). An unproved separation or Label Cover hypothesis cannot be treated as established in an answer to this unconditional question. Hardness for five colours alone, fixed-point-logic inexpressibility, an algorithm with a growing palette, partial colouring, or a restricted input family does not settle the full target.
why: A defining promise-CSP problem: determine whether relaxing an NP-hard colouring task to any fixed larger palette permits efficient construction of a valid solution.

importance.reason: The paradigmatic approximate graph-colouring question, central to promise CSPs and to the gap between algorithmic relaxations and hardness with perfect completeness.

progress.text: Barto–Bulín–Krokhin–Opršal establish the NP-hardness of five-colouring three-colourable graphs; the full work appears in JACM in 2021.
Guruswami–Sandeep derive hardness for every fixed output palette from a d-to-1 conjecture with perfect completeness.
Kawarabayashi–Thorup–Yoneda obtain \(\widetilde O(n^{0.19747})\) colours using improved combinatorial progress combined with SDP methods.
Bansal–Huang–Lee improve the general polynomial-time upper bound to \(O(n^{0.19539})\) colours through a new SDP-based analysis.
The revised Dawar–Molnár full version proves an all-constant obstruction for fixed-point logic with counting; it does not establish unrestricted computational hardness.

A new preprint claims NP-hardness for every fixed three-versus-k decision gap. Its full proof is not audited here, and even the asserted hardness alone would not unconditionally settle randomized algorithm existence.

status_note: The exact randomized constant-palette algorithm question remains source-open in this review. A new14September2026 preprint, Fei–Minzer–Wang ECCC TR26-179, claims in Corollary1.7 unconditional NP-hardness of every fixed three-versus-k decision gap. On16September2026 its introductory definitions, main theorem and exact corollary were checked; its95-page proof was not independently audited. Even if that claimed theorem is established, ruling out the randomized algorithms quantified here additionally requires NP different from RP. Thus it is important new claimed hardness evidence, not an unconditional resolution of this algorithm-existence target. Older references describing six-colour decision hardness as open are historical accounts superseded by this claim.

context_blocks.text: The input comes with a guarantee that three colours suffice, but not with the partition into three independent sets. Allowing more colours is a relaxation of the output requirements. The question asks whether some fixed amount of this relaxation makes the problem efficiently solvable on every promised input. A mechanism for choosing 100 colours would qualify just as a mechanism for choosing six colours would; the constant need not be close to three.

This promise matters. Strong inapproximability results for the chromatic number on unrestricted graphs can use instances whose chromatic number grows with the graph size. They do not automatically establish hardness when the yes-instances must have chromatic number at most three. Conversely, an algorithm for planar graphs would use a structural assumption missing here. Three-colourable graphs can be dense and can have high-degree vertices.

The problem is a basic example of promise constraint satisfaction. An edge asks its two endpoints to receive different labels. The promise says the constraints have a solution over a three-element domain; the algorithm is allowed to use a larger fixed domain. In graph-homomorphism language, an input maps to \(K_{3}\) and the output must provide a map to \(K_{C}\). The associated decision promise distinguishes graphs mapping to \(K_{3}\) from graphs not mapping to \(K_{C}\).

The algebraic PCSP theorem gives unconditional NP-hardness of the three-versus-five decision gap. A randomized five-colouring search algorithm with the guarantee in this card would yield an RP algorithm for SAT after applying the reduction and checking its output, so excluding such a randomized algorithm requires \(\mathsf{NP}\ne\mathsf{RP}\). Here RP means polynomial time with no accepting computation on a NO-instance and acceptance probability at least one half on every YES-instance. The result addresses only small fixed palettes, leaving six, one hundred and every other larger constant unexcluded by that theorem alone.

A useful elementary observation is that the neighbours of any vertex in a three-colourable graph induce a bipartite graph: the vertex’s own colour cannot appear among its neighbours. Thus one can efficiently colour a large neighbourhood using two fresh colours. When all remaining degrees are small, greedy colouring is effective. Balancing these two procedures already gives an \(O(\sqrt{n})\)-colour algorithm. The challenge is to extract much more global information than this local observation provides.

Modern algorithms combine combinatorial reductions with semidefinite relaxations. The relaxation assigns vectors that mimic the separation of colours, and rounding extracts independent sets or other useful progress. Kawarabayashi, Thorup and Yoneda’s STOC 2024 work strengthens the combinatorial side and obtains \(\widetilde O(n^{0.19747})\) colours after combining it with the SDP approach. The suppressed factors are polylogarithmic in n.

Bansal, Huang and Lee’s February 2026 preprint improves the SDP analysis using third-level neighbourhoods and a new vector \(5/2\)-colouring construction. Combined with the combinatorial component, its theorem gives \(O(n^{0.19539})\) colours. A vector \(5/2\)-colouring is a geometric relaxation, not an ordinary assignment using a fractional number of colours. The exponent improvement is real progress, while the final number of actual colours still grows with n.

Hardness evidence also goes beyond five colours under additional assumptions. Guruswami and Sandeep show that a fixed d-to-1 Label Cover conjecture implies hardness for every constant output palette. Their premise requires perfectly satisfiable yes-instances. Replacing perfect completeness by near-perfect completeness changes what the reduction guarantees, so established results about almost-satisfiable games cannot simply be substituted into this argument.

Dawar and Molnár’s full version, revised in March 2026, proves that fixed-point logic with counting cannot separate three-colourable graphs from graphs requiring more than any fixed number of colours. This is an unconditional obstruction for that logic on unordered structures, not for all polynomial-time algorithms on explicitly encoded graphs. The card sits at the intersection of approximation algorithms, algebraic reductions and limits of relaxation methods: a resolution would tell us how much a fixed expansion of the solution domain can help.

Fixed-point logic with counting augments first-order descriptions by iterative fixed points and counting operators. On unordered graphs it does not express every polynomial-time algorithm available on an explicit binary encoding. Thus the March 2026 theorem is an unconditional limitation of a powerful logic, but a different machine using the encoding’s order is not covered.

The14September2026 Fei–Minzer–Wang preprint claims a perfectly complete4-to-1 game theorem and, in Corollary1.7, NP-hardness of every fixed three-versus-k colouring gap. Its complete proof has not been independently audited here. If established, this removes the extra Label Cover conjecture from that hardness claim, but excluding the randomized search algorithms in this card would still require NP different from RP. The distinction follows because candidate colourings are efficiently checkable, giving one-sided error after a gap reduction.
